In Memory of Plants

Galiano Island lies within the unceded traditional territories of the Penelakut, Lamalcha, Hwlitsum and other Hul’q’umi’num-speaking peoples, who have cared for these lands and waters since time immemorial.

The memory preserved here is much more limited: collected specimens, names written down on lists, and observations shared through iNaturalist, reaching back to 1958.

Each record is a moment when someone stopped to take note of a plant.

Some plants have long been recorded, while others have appeared only in more recent years. Still others have gone unseen for decades, quietly disappearing from the record.

The lost plants of Galiano Island

This gallery shows native species once reported for Galiano Island, which have not been seen in recent decades. Some may be lost to us—overlooked, forgotten, or waiting to be rediscovered. Others may be lost because of us, through impacts like habitat change or the introduction of invasive species.

Select a plant from the gallery to read its curatorial notes, then explore its distribution on the Atlas, or add curatorial notes in Living Data. Then join local naturalists and community members on a search for it through the Biodiversity Galiano Island project on iNaturalist.

These native species were reported for the island in the past, and have been seen again since 2004. They represent the enduring core of its native flora—though being found again is no promise of security, and some plants are known to occur in only one or two places.

Select a plant from the gallery to read its curatorial notes, then explore its distribution on the Atlas, or add curatorial notes in Living Data.

These native species were first reported for Galiano Island since 2004. Some were surely here all along, overlooked by earlier botanists or confused with their relatives; others may be new arrivals or newly recognized taxonomically.

Select a plant from the gallery to read its curatorial notes, then explore its distribution on the Atlas, or add curatorial notes in Living Data.

Not every plant reported for the island is an accepted part of its flora. Some plants have been excluded for various reasons: curators have judged some to be doubtful reports, others to be garden escapes that persist without establishing.

Select a plant from the gallery to read curatorial notes.

Herbarium collections at the Royal BC Museum and UBC, and Harvey Janszen’s (2003) Outer Gulf Islands Vascular Plant Checklist, provide the historical baseline for this atlas. Harvey passed away in 2021, and a community of naturalists has since carried his work forward through Biodiversity Galiano; this atlas is a testament to that continuing legacy.

Flora of Galiano Island

To date, 812 vascular plant species have been recorded on Galiano Island, drawing together 24734 records from historical collections, iNaturalist observations and other sources. Each species falls into one of three groups:

Click a group to show only the records of those species, old and recent, on the map and in the list. Open Filters to narrow records by recorder, locality or time period, pick a plant from the list to see only its records, or use the shape tool at the top left of the map to draw an area, double-clicking to finish. Open Records below the map for the details behind each selection.

Community contributions to our knowledge of the island’s plant diversity

Through the combined efforts of 767 individuals, the Galiano naturalist community has now documented a total of 812 vascular plant species. Since 2004, 83 percent of the historically reported plant diversity has been confirmed and 207 new species reports added to the list.

Through iNaturalist alone, community members have now documented 85 percent of the plant diversity known to the island.

Contribute to this growing record by submitting your observations to the Biodiversity Galiano Island iNaturalist project.

Here, you can browse photos of some of the most commonly documented plants, as well as recent observations and top observers across the island, based on iNaturalist data. Visualisation code courtesy of Ben Keen.

Finding the lost plants

Every plant in this list is a search waiting to happen. This tool suggests where to begin from the pattern of past sightings alone, applying one component of our protocol for detecting local extinction.

Extirpation probability (EP) runs from 0 (likely still present) to 1 (likely lost locally). Using Solow’s (1993) method, it compares when a species was sighted with the whole period of record, from the earliest collection in our data (1958) to 2025. EP is highest for plants that were recorded repeatedly and then stopped being seen. Plants recorded only once or twice tend to score nearer the middle, since so few records say little either way.

Five steps to a target species:

  1. Choose a plant. The table lists the highest EP first. Tick a species, and use Filters to narrow the list, for example to native species.
  2. See where it grew. Each circle on the map is a group of sightings treated as one population, coloured by its EP. Hover over one for its Cluster EP. A smaller Population radius can reveal sites where a plant has gone unseen even though it persists elsewhere. A ⚠ marks plants with records that have no coordinates and so cannot be mapped.
  3. Read its history. Open Records to see who found it, when and where. The dates show what time of year it was collected.
  4. Go looking. Search the places and habitats where it was last recorded, at the season it was last seen.
  5. Share what you find. Post your photos to iNaturalist through the Biodiversity Galiano Island project. Whatever you find, the search itself adds to what we know.

A high EP is a reason to go looking, not proof of loss. It does not account for where or how hard people have searched, or for suitable habitat, which the full protocol goes on to weigh.

Native plant diversity within protected areas

All protected areasUnprotected native plant diversity

All protected and conserved areas

Based on our current knowledge, 86 percent of the 438 native vascular plant species known to the island have been reported within its protected and conserved areas, from provincial parks and its ecological reserve to the lands held by the Galiano Conservancy Association, the Islands Trust Conservancy, the Galiano Club and other conservancies. The other 63 have so far been recorded only outside them.

This preliminary evaluation is limited by biases in sampling effort and other gaps in the data, but it is a starting point for a more thorough assessment of progress toward conserving the region’s plant diversity. Help improve it by reporting your observations to the Biodiversity Galiano Island iNaturalist project.

The map shows protected and conserved areas by category. Galiano Island has as yet no published Key Biodiversity Area, but two are proposed - Mount Sutil & Mount Galiano Bluffs, and Active Pass - and since their boundaries are not yet public, each is marked by a ring at its point. Click an area on the map, or in the chart below it, to show only the plants recorded there and its summary above, or a category in the map’s legend or the chart to show those recorded in all its areas. Choose Unprotected native plant diversity in the chart to show, as a grid on the map, where the native plants not yet reported in any protected area have been recorded. Protected areas are from the Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database (Environment and Climate Change Canada), and Key Biodiversity Areas from KBA Canada (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

Harvey’s footsteps

This project is dedicated to the memory of Harvey Janszen (July 11, 1946–May 10, 2021) and other fellow naturalists, including Hans Roemer, who have passed away in recent years. Harvey spent decades getting to know the plants of the Salish Sea—collecting more than 3000 plant specimens, keeping field journals from 1973 to 2017, and compiling species checklists for the southern Gulf Islands, the Saanich Peninsula, and the San Juan Islands.

Galiano Island was part of Harvey’s botanical life from his very first journal, which records collections from Galiano alongside those of Saturna and the neighbouring islands, through to his later inventories of the island’s rock bluffs and meadows. His Outer Gulf Islands Vascular Plant Checklist (2003) remains a cornerstone of this flora: together with his specimens, it accounts for 806 of the records in this atlas, documenting 542 of Galiano’s plants between 1973 and 2003. The photograph above was taken on Galiano Island on May 3, 2019.

Through the Janszen Legacy Project we continue to digitize Harvey’s journals and collections, and through this atlas we invite you to help carry his work forward, by sharing your local plant knowledge and contributing to the co-creation of a living Flora of Galiano Island.
